bands.title: Below the screening threshold
bands.summary: Your answers fall well below the ASRS screening threshold of 14. They do not suggest frequent ADHD-related experiences over the past six months.

bands.title: Below the screening threshold, with some symptoms
bands.summary: Your answers are below the screening threshold of 14, although some ADHD-related experiences seem to happen fairly often.

bands.title: At or above the screening threshold
bands.summary: Your answers are at or above the ASRS screening threshold of 14. Some of these experiences may be worth discussing with a qualified professional. This is not a diagnosis.

bands.title: Well above the screening threshold
bands.summary: Your answers are well above the ASRS screening threshold. Consider discussing these experiences with a doctor or qualified professional, who can carry out a full assessment. This is not a diagnosis.

support.text: A positive screen is a starting point, not an answer. A doctor, psychiatrist or psychologist can carry out a full ADHD assessment and also consider other explanations, such as stress, sleep or anxiety.

inattention.low: Finishing, organising and remembering tasks rarely seem to be a problem for you.
inattention.moderate: You sometimes find it hard to finish, organise or start demanding tasks.
inattention.high: Finishing details, getting organised, remembering appointments or starting demanding tasks often seem difficult.
inattention.reflect: Which kinds of tasks are hardest for you to start or finish?
inattention.tip: Use reminders outside your head, such as alarms, lists or a calendar, so your memory doesn't have to do all the work.

hyperactivity.moderate: You sometimes feel fidgety or driven to keep moving.
hyperactivity.high: You often feel restless or driven to keep moving, especially when sitting for long periods.
hyperactivity.reflect: When do you feel most restless?
hyperactivity.tip: Build short movement breaks into long periods of sitting.

focus.low: Your attention usually stays where you want it.
focus.moderate: Your mind sometimes wanders or gets pulled away by distractions.
focus.high: Distractions and a wandering mind often pull you away from what you are doing.
focus.reflect: When is it easiest for you to focus, and what is different then?
focus.tip: Try short focus blocks (for example 20 minutes) with notifications switched off.

organisation.low: Keeping track of things and routines rarely causes problems.
organisation.moderate: Belongings, clutter or routine steps sometimes slip through.
organisation.high: Misplacing things, clutter or forgotten steps often make daily life harder.
organisation.reflect: Which everyday item or task causes you the most friction?
organisation.tip: Give important items one fixed home, such as a tray by the door for keys and wallet.

time_management.low: You usually estimate time well and stay on schedule.
time_management.moderate: Time sometimes gets away from you, especially with bigger tasks.
time_management.high: Time often slips away, leading to lateness or last-minute rushes.
time_management.reflect: Which tasks do you most often underestimate?
time_management.tip: Add a buffer: plan for tasks to take about one and a half times as long as you expect.

impulsivity.low: You usually pause before speaking or deciding.
impulsivity.moderate: Now and then you act or speak before thinking it through.
impulsivity.high: You often act, speak or buy on impulse and sometimes regret it later.
impulsivity.reflect: In what situations do you find it hardest to pause?
impulsivity.tip: Before a non-urgent purchase or reply, try a short pause rule, such as waiting 10 minutes.

restlessness.low: You can usually settle and relax during quiet time.
restlessness.moderate: You sometimes feel fidgety or need to move during quiet moments.
restlessness.high: You often feel a strong need to move and find quiet time hard.
restlessness.reflect: What kinds of movement help you feel settled?
restlessness.tip: Plan movement into your day, such as a walk before tasks that need you to sit still.

suggestions: Your ASRS score comes only from questions 1-6. The everyday pattern areas are extra self-reflection and are not part of the screener.
ADHD-like experiences can also come from stress, poor sleep, anxiety or low mood.
Only a qualified professional can assess ADHD, through a full evaluation.
Practical tools like timers, checklists and working alongside someone can help, with or without a diagnosis.
note: ASRS screener (questions 1-6), scored using the Harvard ASRS v1.1 scoring update (2024): Never = 0, Rarely = 1, Sometimes = 2, Often = 3, Very often = 4, summed to 0-24. A total of 14 or more is a positive screen. Bands: 0-9 low negative, 10-13 high negative, 14-17 low positive, 18-24 high positive. Everyday patterns (questions 7-20) are MindCheck self-reflection questions. Each area is shown on a 0-100 scale; they are not validated and never change the ASRS score. 'Attention & organisation' and 'Restlessness & activity' come from the ASRS questions.
